draft.title: FamilyBench: Exploring LLMs' Ability to Handle Complex Family Tree Reasoning
draft.body: FamilyBench is an open-source benchmark designed to test large language models on understanding complex, tree-like family relationships within a massive context. It uses a Python program to generate a family tree and then formulates questions based on that structure. Initial tests involved seven models, including six open-weight and one closed, tackling a 400-person tree spanning 10 generations and about 18,000 tokens. Models answered 200 questions each, with testing done via OpenRouter under parameters like 8k max tokens and a temperature of 0.3. Reported results show accuracy ranging from around 64% to over 81%, with Gemini 2.5 Pro leading at 81.48% accuracy and zero no-response rate. However, these early results come with caveats: the benchmark is new, testing parameters may not be optimal for all models, and the no-response rate reflects token limits rather than outright failures. For those interested in local LLM development, it raises questions about how to improve reasoning over large, structured contexts and whether fine-tuning or different prompting strategies could boost performance. What approaches might help models better navigate such intricate relational data? And how might FamilyBench evolve to provide deeper insights into LLM reasoning?

draft.title: Discussing FamilyBench: A New Benchmark for Complex Family Tree Reasoning in LLMs
draft.body: FamilyBench offers a novel way to evaluate LLMs on complex family tree reasoning by generating a large, multi-generation tree and asking models detailed questions about it. The initial benchmark tested seven models on a 400-person tree with about 18k tokens, asking 200 questions each. Testing used OpenRouter with low reasoning effort settings and a temperature of 0.3, which might not be ideal for all models. Results varied, with Gemini 2.5 Pro achieving the highest accuracy (~81%) and no instances of running out of tokens, while others like GLM 4.5 had lower accuracy and some no-response cases. Given these early findings, I'm curious about what factors most influence model performance here—context window size, prompt design, or model architecture? Also, how might the benchmark's question generation and tree complexity evolve to better challenge LLMs? For those experimenting locally, what strategies have you found effective in pushing models to handle such large, structured relational data?
